name: Scapula
func: The shoulder blade: a flat, triangular bone on the upper back. It forms the socket of the shoulder joint and anchors 17 muscles, gliding over the ribs so the arm can reach in almost any direction.

levels.kid:
Your **scapula** is your **shoulder blade**. Reach one hand over your shoulder and pat your upper back: the flat bone you feel is your scapula. You have one on each side.

It's shaped like a triangle, kind of like a flat slice of pizza. It's not glued to your back bone; it slides around on top of your ribs, held in place by lots of muscles.

Your scapula has a little cup on its side. The round top of your arm bone sits in that cup, which makes your shoulder joint.

When you reach up high, throw a ball or do a cartwheel, your scapula slides and spins to help your arm move. It's like a moving platform for your arm!
levels.hs:
The **scapula** (shoulder blade) is a flat, triangular bone lying on the back of the rib cage, over ribs 2 to 7. It has **three borders** (medial, lateral, superior) and **three angles** (superior, inferior, lateral).

Key parts:
- The **spine of the scapula**, a ridge across the back, which you can feel. It ends in a flat projection, the **acromion**, which forms the tip of the shoulder and joins the clavicle at the **AC joint**.
- The **coracoid process**, a hook-like projection pointing forward under the clavicle.
- The **glenoid cavity**, a shallow oval socket at the lateral angle, which meets the head of the **humerus** to form the **shoulder (glenohumeral) joint**.
- The **supraspinous** and **infraspinous fossae** above and below the spine, and the **subscapular fossa** on the front surface facing the ribs.

The scapula is not attached to the spine by a joint. Instead, it moves over the chest wall at the **scapulothoracic** articulation, held by muscles such as the trapezius, rhomboids and **serratus anterior**. It anchors the four **rotator cuff** muscles that keep the arm bone centred in its shallow socket.
levels.college:
**Rotator cuff (SITS)** origins on the scapula, all inserting on the humerus:
- **Supraspinatus** (supraspinous fossa): starts abduction; suprascapular nerve.
- **Infraspinatus** (infraspinous fossa): lateral rotation; suprascapular nerve.
- **Teres minor** (lateral border): lateral rotation; axillary nerve.
- **Subscapularis** (subscapular fossa): medial rotation; upper and lower subscapular nerves.

Other attachments: **deltoid** from the spine and acromion; **long head of biceps** from the **supraglenoid tubercle**; **long head of triceps** from the **infraglenoid tubercle**; **short head of biceps**, **coracobrachialis** and **pectoralis minor** at the coracoid; **teres major** near the inferior angle.

The **suprascapular notch** on the superior border is bridged by the **superior transverse scapular ligament**: the **suprascapular nerve** passes under it and the **artery** over it ("the army goes over the bridge, the navy goes under").

The **glenoid** is deepened by a fibrocartilage rim, the **glenoid labrum**. Arm elevation combines glenohumeral movement and scapular upward rotation in roughly a **2:1 ratio** (**scapulohumeral rhythm**); the trapezius (upper and lower parts) and serratus anterior rotate the scapula upward so the arm can go overhead.

Surface landmarks: the root of the scapular spine is at about **T3**, and the **inferior angle** is at about **T7**. The scapula is surrounded by an arterial anastomosis (suprascapular, dorsal scapular and circumflex scapular arteries) that can bypass a blocked axillary artery.
levels.phd:
The scapula has a dual embryonic origin. Fate-mapping in chick and mouse shows the **blade** comes largely from **somitic (dermomyotome-derived)** cells, while the glenoid region, coracoid and spine derive from **lateral plate mesoderm**. Genes such as **Pax1**, **Emx2**, **Tbx15** and **Pbx1** pattern the scapula, and mutations cause scapular hypoplasia or absent blades. It ossifies from one primary centre in the body plus several secondary centres (coracoid, acromion, glenoid rim, inferior angle, medial border) that fuse by about the early twenties; failure of the acromial centres to fuse produces an **os acromiale**, seen in a few percent of people and easily mistaken for a fracture.

The **glenoid** is shallow and covers only about a third of the humeral head, giving the shoulder the largest range of movement of any joint at the cost of stability. Stability relies on the **concavity–compression** mechanism of the rotator cuff, the labrum (which increases socket depth substantially), negative intra-articular pressure and the glenohumeral ligaments.

**Scapular dyskinesis**, abnormal scapular position or motion, is a focus of shoulder research. EMG studies show coordinated firing of serratus anterior and lower trapezius drives upward rotation and posterior tilt; altered activation is linked to impingement and throwing injuries. 3D motion analysis with bone-pin or biplane fluoroscopy has shown that the scapula also tilts and rotates internally/externally, not just upward.

Acromion shape (Bigliani types I–III, flat to hooked) was proposed as a cause of rotator cuff disease; current evidence suggests intrinsic tendon degeneration with age matters more, and some acromial spurs may be a consequence rather than the cause.
levels.expert:
**Winged scapula** is a classic neurological sign:
- **Medial winging**: the medial border lifts off the chest when pushing against a wall, from **serratus anterior** weakness due to **long thoracic nerve** (C5–C7) injury, e.g. after carrying heavy backpacks, trauma or surgery on the side of the chest.
- **Lateral winging**: from **trapezius** weakness due to **spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)** injury, a known risk of neck lymph node surgery in the posterior triangle; there is also shoulder droop and difficulty shrugging.

**Suprascapular nerve entrapment** at the notch (from a ganglion cyst or ligament) weakens supraspinatus and infraspinatus; compression at the **spinoglenoid notch** spares supraspinatus, causing isolated infraspinatus wasting. **EMG/nerve conduction** studies and **MRI** confirm, and surgical release may help.

**Scapular fractures** need high-energy trauma, so they flag possible associated chest injuries (rib fractures, pneumothorax, lung contusion) and should prompt a careful CT. Most are treated without surgery; displaced glenoid fractures may need fixation.

**Shoulder dislocation** usually goes anterior; it can tear the labrum (**Bankart lesion**) or chip the glenoid rim (bony Bankart). Recurrent instability may need arthroscopic labral repair or a **Latarjet procedure**, which transfers the coracoid to the front of the glenoid.

On exam, compare scapular position and muscle bulk from behind; check for supraspinatus and infraspinatus wasting. Imaging: X-ray views (AP, scapular Y, axillary), CT for fracture patterns and MRI for cuff and labrum.

keyPoints: Flat triangular bone over ribs 2–7; moves over the chest wall
Parts: spine, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity
Suprascapular artery over the ligament, nerve under
Medial winging = long thoracic nerve; lateral winging = accessory nerve

test.q: Which part of the scapula forms the socket of the shoulder joint?
test.explain: The humeral head sits in the shallow glenoid cavity.

test.q: Medial winging of the scapula is caused by injury to which nerve?
test.explain: It supplies serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the ribs.

test.q: Name the rotator cuff muscle that lies in the supraspinous fossa.
test.explain: Supraspinatus starts abduction and is the most commonly torn cuff tendon.

test.q: Which passes UNDER the superior transverse scapular ligament?
test.explain: Army (artery) over the bridge, navy (nerve) under.

test.q: The beak-like projection of the scapula pointing forward under the clavicle is the ______ process.
test.explain: It anchors pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps.
